#786. A nuclear blast could save Earth from an asteroid, but there's a catch

A nuclear explosion could potentially protect Earth from an incoming asteroid by releasing powerful X-rays that heat its surface and push it onto a safer trajectory. However, new research suggests that the success of such a mission could depend heavily on which side of the asteroid receives the blast.

Unlike the smooth, round objects often used in computer simulations, real asteroids have uneven surfaces and irregular shapes. Those differences can dramatically influence how an asteroid moves when exposed to intense radiation.

A new study published in Icarus found that changing the direction of an X-ray burst could produce vastly different results, even when targeting the same asteroid. In one simulation, the asteroid's speed changed by 3.9 millimeters per second when irradiated from one direction, compared with only 0.8 millimeters per second from another. That represents a nearly fivefold difference in deflection velocity, the change in the asteroid's forward speed caused by the burst.

"We expected aim to matter," said Nathan Moore, a physicist at Sandia National Laboratories who led the research. "What surprised us was how much."

The effects on an asteroid's rotation could be even more dramatic. For another simulated asteroid, the change in how quickly it spun varied by a factor of 17 depending on the direction of the X-rays.

These findings suggest that understanding an asteroid's shape and carefully selecting where to direct a nuclear blast could be essential to protecting Earth from a future impact.

The research received funding through Sandia's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program.

A New Way to Simulate Asteroid Deflection

To investigate how different asteroid shapes respond to nuclear blasts, Moore and his colleagues developed what they describe as the most accurate asteroid deflection model yet.

Earlier computer models faced a major limitation. Researchers typically had to choose between representing an asteroid's complex shape and performing highly detailed calculations of the physical forces involved. Combining both approaches demanded more computing power than was practical.

The new system overcomes that obstacle, allowing scientists to study realistic asteroid shapes while maintaining the precision needed to calculate their response to an X-ray burst. The result is the most detailed simulation of asteroid deflection produced so far.

"Our new algorithm is over 1,600 times faster, which was critical to this breakthrough," Moore said. "With the old models, computers just couldn't handle it."

Moore's interest in improving these calculations grew out of an earlier experiment using Sandia's Z machine. That experiment provided the first demonstration that X-rays could deflect a small piece of asteroid material.

The next challenge was determining how the same physical process might affect an entire asteroid.

"I started wondering how to scale up the calculation to more accurately predict deflection of a full-scale asteroid."

A major problem was the widespread practice of treating asteroids as spheres. Although this simplifies the mathematics, it overlooks the irregular shapes of real asteroids, which can have ridges, depressions, and uneven surfaces.

"You can make estimates that way, but asteroids come in all kinds of odd, lumpy shapes," he said. "That's when I latched onto some work one of my colleagues was doing related to outgassing of objects in space. I think we had an aha moment when we realized we could do this. No more spheres. We would be able to model deflection for any asteroid."

The solution involved bringing together two sophisticated simulation systems already used at Sandia for very different types of physical problems.

"The ALEGRA code is normally used to model fast, high-energy experiments, like magnetically imploding wires on the Z machine, while SPARTA, a direct simulation Monte Carlo code, is usually used to model comparatively weak, slowly evolving forces, like the drag on a satellite from the solar wind," Moore explained.

"The key innovation here was figuring out how to combine the two simulation approaches."

Predicting What Happens After a Nuclear Blast

The new computer model allows researchers to reconstruct an asteroid using detailed 3D images captured during spacecraft flybys. They can then simulate a nuclear X-ray burst while adjusting the explosion's strength, its distance from the asteroid, and the direction from which the radiation arrives.

The software calculates how much material would vaporize across different parts of the asteroid's surface and displays the results as a heat map. Using that information, it estimates the resulting push, changes in the asteroid's rotation, and the extent of surface damage.

These calculations are important because a successful planetary defense mission would ideally change an asteroid's trajectory without breaking it into multiple dangerous fragments. Redirecting one large object could be preferable to creating several pieces that might still threaten Earth.

However, the simulations cannot yet predict every possible consequence of a nuclear blast.

"Right now, our computer model only considers breakup of rocks on the surface. We can't predict breakup of the entire asteroid body accurately yet," Moore said.

Developing that capability will require additional research, investment, and more advanced computational tools. An intense X-ray burst can trigger numerous physical effects, some of which influence one another. Accounting for all those interactions makes it exceptionally difficult to predict exactly how an asteroid would behave during a real deflection attempt.

Choosing the Right Blast Could Save Earth

Despite these remaining challenges, the findings offer valuable guidance for future planetary defense efforts. The research shows that the direction of a nuclear blast is not simply a minor detail. It can substantially change how effectively an asteroid is redirected.

"Our study shows how important it is to aim carefully," Moore said. "Pick the right side and you win. Guess wrong and it could be a bad day."

The new simulation tools could eventually help mission planners identify the most effective way to deflect a threatening asteroid. In principle, researchers could enter detailed information about its shape, then calculate the ideal explosive strength, distance, and direction needed to move it away from Earth.

Turning those calculations into a real mission would still be extremely difficult.

For one thing, the software requires reasonably accurate information about the asteroid's shape from every direction. If an asteroid were discovered on a collision course with Earth, there might not be enough time to gather the necessary observations.

Another challenge would be delivering and positioning a nuclear device at precisely the right location relative to an asteroid traveling through space. Even if scientists could identify the ideal blast configuration, executing it would require extraordinary precision.

Nevertheless, the improved simulations could eliminate much of the uncertainty surrounding one possible method of asteroid defense. By better understanding how nuclear X-rays interact with the complex surfaces of real asteroids, scientists are moving closer to predicting which strategies would work best.

For Moore, that progress is an encouraging step toward ensuring humanity has a better chance of preventing a catastrophic asteroid impact.

#785. RAYE & Rosalía Lead 2027 Grammy Nominations as Women Make History

Also, for the first time in Grammy history, seven artists are nominated for album, record and song of the year.

RAYE is the leading artist in the 2027 Grammy nominations, with 11 nods, tying Beyoncé’s record set two years ago for the most nods by a woman in one year. But the story goes way beyond RAYE.

For the first time in Grammy history, the six artists with the most nominations are all women. RAYE is followed by Rosalía with nine nods, and then Phoebe Bridgers, Miranda Lambert, Ella Langley and Olivia Rodrigo with seven each. (For the record, the male artists with the most nominations are Bruno Mars and Leon Thomas, with six each.)

Seven of the album of the year nominees are by women artists, which matches the record set in 2024, when the nominees included six female solo artists and one all-female group (boygenius). Three of the same women were nominated in both years: Bridgers (as part of boygenius then; solo now), Rodrigo and Taylor Swift.

Also, for the first time in Grammy history, seven artists are nominated for album, record and song of the year: Olivia Dean, Langley, Mars, RAYE, Rodrigo, Rosalía and Swift. Langley is also nominated for best new artist. She’s the first country artist to be nominated in each of the four highest-profile categories since Bobbie Gentry in 1968.

This is the fifth time Swift has been nominated for album, record and song of the year in the same year, which sets a new record. It’s the third time that Mars and Rodrigo have achieved this feat.

Rosalía becomes the second Latin artist to be nominated for album, record and song of the year in the same year. Bad Bunny achieved the feat last year with his album Debí Tirar Más Fotos and single “DTMF.” Rosalía is nominated for record and song of the year for “Berghain,” a collab with Björk and Yves Tumor. That collab dramatizes the increased globalization of pop music. Rosalía is from Spain. Her featured artists are from Iceland and the U.S., respectively. The song is performed in German, Spanish and English.

Mars and Swift are each nominated with different songs in record and song of the year. Mars made it with “I Just Might” in record and “Risk It All” in song. Swift is competing with “The Fate of Ophelia” in record and “I Knew It, I Knew You” in song.

Swift’s The Life of a Showgirl is her eighth album to receive an album of the year nod – more than anyone else in Grammy history for strictly solo albums. Moreover, it’s her fifth consecutive studio album to be nominated (not counting Taylor’s Version re-recordings). She’s only the second artist (following Kendrick Lamar) to be nominated for album of the year with five consecutive studio albums.

In song of the year, Swift and her collaborator Jack Antonoff are nominated for their Disney tune “I Knew It, I Knew You.” It’s the ninth nomination in the category for the frequent collaborators, extending their shared record as the songwriters with the most nominations in the category. The only disappointment for Swift is that The Life of a Showgirl was passed over for a nod for best pop vocal album. It’s the second time she has received an album of the year nod for an album that failed to receive a nod in a genre album category. The same fate befell Evermore.

“I Just Might” is Mars’ eighth record of the year nod as an artist. Only Beyoncé has had more (nine). (In addition, Mars was nominated as a producer of Cee Lo Green’s “F**k You (Forget You)”).

Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” is the first song by a core country artist performing a country song to receive a record of the year nod since Lady A won for “Need You Now” in 2011. Langley’s Dandelion is the first album by a core country artist to land an album of the year nod since Kacey Musgraves’ Golden Hour, which won in 2019.

Tame Impala’s “Dracula” (featuring JENNIE) is up for record of the year. This is the second year in a row that a member of Blackpink has been nominated in that high-profile category. ROSÉ was nominated last year for her Bruno Mars collab, “APT.” (Oddly, Blackpink has yet to receive a Grammy nomination.)

Ariana Grande receives four nominations, including her first song of the year nod for “hate that i made you love me,” and her record seventh nod for best pop vocal album for Petal. She surpasses Swift and Kelly Clarkson, who have each received six nods in that category. (Swift would have kept pace with Grande if Showgirl had been nominated.)

Beyoncé becomes the first artist to receive 100 career Grammy nominations as “Morning Dew (Donk)” is nominated for best R&B solo performance. She is followed on the Grammy nominations leaderboard by Jay-Z (89 nods) and Paul McCartney, whose nominations total advances to 86 this year.

The late Dolly Parton receives three nominations, the most she has amassed in any one year since 1982, when her smash “9 to 5” led to four nominations. Parton has two nominations for best country duo/group performance for “Light of a Clear Blue Morning” (featuring Lainey Wilson, Miley Cyrus, Queen Latifah and Reba McEntire) and Zac Brown Band’s “Butterfly” (on which she is featured). She’s also nominated for best audio book, narration, and storytelling recording. (More on that category below.)

Three veteran artists make a strong showing in the nominations. Madonna receives four nods, the most she has received in any one year since 1999, when she nabbed five. Her latest album Confessions II is nominated for best dance electronic album. The Rolling Stones and McCartney each receive three nods. The Stones are up for best rock album for Foreign Tongues. McCartney is up for best traditional pop vocal album for The Boys of Dungeon Lane.

Lambert, nominated as a producer on Langley’s single and album, is nominated for producer of the year, non-classical. Lambert is the first woman to be nominated in that category since Alissia two years ago. The other nominees in the category are Dernst “D Mile” Emile II (his fourth nod) and Tony Berg, Noah Goldstein and Mike Sabath (their first in each case).

Amy Allen and Edgar Barrera are nominated for songwriter of the year, non-classical for the fourth time (out of the five years the category has been presented). RAYE and Theron Thomas are each nominated for the second time in the category. Joybeth Taylor, a collaborator on “Choosin’ Texas,” is nominated for the first time.

In addition to dominating the Big Four categories, women completely own several categories. All five nominees for best dance pop recording (Zara Larsson, Madonna, RAYE, Slayyyter and Tinashe) are women, as are all five nominees for best R&B solo performance (Beyoncé, Kehlani, Victoria Monét, Jill Scott and Tems) and best contemporary country album (Kelsea Ballerini, Carter Faith, Ella Langley, Megan Moroney and Kacey Musgraves).

The Wizard of Oz at Sphere is nominated for best compilation soundtrack for visual media. It’s not the first time an album from a Las Vegas stage production has been nominated in this category. In 2008, The Beatles’ Love won the award. Love was a theatrical production by Cirque du Soleil which combined the music of The Beatles with a lavish stage performance. The show played at a specially-built theatre at the Mirage on the Las Vegas strip.

The Broadway cast album from Schmigadoon! is nominated for best musical theater album, five years after Schmigadoon! Episode 1, from the property’s initial incarnation as an Apple+ TV series, was nominated for best compilation soundtrack for visual media.

Two former Grammy winners for best new artist (Olivia Dean and Olivia Rodrigo) are nominated for album of the year, as are four artists who were nominated for best new artist but lost. They are: Rosalía (who lost best new artist to Billie Eilish), Phoebe Bridgers (lost to Megan Thee Stallion), RAYE (lost to Chappell Roan), and Taylor Swift (lost to Amy Winehouse).

Elton John’s Billboard 200-topping 1975 album Captain Fantastic & the Brown Dirt Cowboy was nominated for both album of the year and best pop vocal performance, male back in the day. This year, a 50th Anniversary Edition of the album is nominated for best immersive audio album.

The most competitive category? It may just be best audio book, narration, and storytelling recording. Voters must choose between a beloved star who has faced physical hardship with dignity and humor (Michael J. Fox), a widely admired former First Lady (Michelle Obama), a former Beatle (Paul McCartney), two stars who died this year (country legend Dolly Parton and actor/singer Tim Curry) and a hot rapper/record producer (Lil Jon). Tough one.

The Vespera III is a premium smart telescope that delivers powerful features like multi-night observation and mosaic technology, rewarding avid astrophotographers who have a serious interest in capturing the night sky.

Excellent deep-sky images with rich colors

Multi-night imaging makes ambitious targets easier

Much more expensive than many of its rivals

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

I’ve spent a lot of time with smart telescopes, from relatively inexpensive Seestar models to the original Vaonis Vespera and the Vespera Pro. They all promise essentially the same thing — you put a telescope outside at night, choose something interesting on your smartphone and let the technology take care of the rest. The Vaonis Vespera 3 does that exceptionally well, but after spending several nights with it, I’m convinced it’s designed for a rather different kind of buyer.

At $2,490/£2,199, this is hardly an impulse purchase for the beginner who’s curious about astronomy – you could buy several perfectly capable smart telescopes for the same money. Yet I found myself increasingly impressed by what the Vespera 3 could achieve, particularly when I returned to the same object over several nights. The images were sharp, the colors were excellent and I almost never had to think about the battery.

That doesn’t mean the experience was flawless. I sometimes spent longer than I’d have liked waiting for the telescope to get ready, but once it began photographing the sky, the Vespera 3 reminded me why I love smart telescopes so much.

One of my favorite things about smart telescopes is watching a photograph develop as more light is collected. What begins as a fairly ordinary patch of stars gradually becomes something much more interesting. First a faint cloud of gas appears, then more structure emerges, and eventually you have an image that, only a few short years ago, would have been difficult to capture without specialist equipment.

With the Vespera 3, I spent several nights photographing the Pleiades (M45), the famous star cluster in Taurus. The Pleiades make an excellent subject for testing a telescope because the stars are bright, but the surrounding nebulosity is much harder to capture convincingly. The Singularity app used to control Vespera 3 stacks each image as it goes, but keeps them in sight as an optional time-lapse, so you can see exactly why you’re spending so much time on one object.

Even better, the Vespera 3’s PerseverENS feature lets you add data to an existing observation over multiple nights (it’s actually called multi-night observation in the app). Instead of having to call it a night or start again every time the weather interrupts an imaging session, you can return to a target and continue building the image over weeks — or years. This is excellent for faint nebulas, but also for anyone who lives somewhere with unpredictable weather.

The Vespera 3 also has CovalENS, Vaonis’s mosaic imaging system, which captures adjacent sections of sky to produce a larger image. That’s helpful for objects such as the Pleiades and large nebulas, which occupy a substantial area of the sky.

Mosaics inevitably take longer than conventional images — if it images six sections of the night sky, it takes six times longer for the same image quality — but they also make the telescope more versatile than its native field of view (2.5 x 1.4 degrees) might suggest.

Smart telescopes are particularly useful for people living under light-polluted skies. A conventional optical telescope can show you the moon, the planets and some brighter star clusters, but faint nebulas are largely out of reach. The Vespera 3 tackles that problem by taking repeated short exposures and combining them automatically. As the exposures accumulate, faint details become clearer, and the image becomes less noisy.

I photographed the Orion Nebula (M42), one of the most rewarding deep-sky targets for almost any telescope. Its bright central region makes it a quick capture, but the surrounding clouds of gas give a camera plenty more to uncover. The color in M42 via the Vespera 3 was particularly striking: stars looked sharp, the background was pleasingly clean, but the colors had a richness you don’t always see from less expensive models.

The Vespera 3 uses a 50mm refractor telescope and an 8.3-megapixel Sony IMX585 camera sensor. Those specifications are identical to the Vespera 2, but the Vespera 3 has a new optical system, which uses four lenses in three groups, including two extra-low-dispersion elements. Vaonis has also introduced internal baffling to reduce unwanted reflections from nearby artificial lights. For urban astronomers, every little helps. I wouldn’t claim that the Vespera 3 makes dark skies unnecessary. It doesn’t — and if you do take a trip to dark skies with the Vespera 3, your images will improve — but it can produce extremely satisfying images even from a city.

For anyone who wants more control over their images, the Vespera 3 also saves lossless TIFF files that can be exported to a PC or Mac using a USB-C cable. That means you can take the images into your preferred editing software for further processing, rather than relying entirely on the results produced by the Singularity app.

There’s something wonderfully simple about looking at a map of the night sky, spotting an interesting object and tapping it to point your scope in that direction. It’s one of the reasons I enjoy using Seestar smart telescopes. I did miss that experience with the Vespera 3.

Vaonis’s Singularity app has an extensive catalog of galaxies, nebulas, star clusters and other targets, but I found myself browsing lists when I’d rather have been exploring an interactive sky chart.

There is a section devoted to constellations, which initially got my hopes up. I thought it might allow me to photograph an entire constellation, capturing its familiar star pattern as a wide-field image. Sadly not — each constellation has a diagram showing where the catalog’s deep-sky objects are located. That’s useful if you already know what you’re looking for, but it isn’t the same as being able to see the sky overhead and choose a target visually.

However, the telescope can still find and photograph the objects in its catalog, and the automated tracking works well once you’ve made your choice.

That smart telescopes give you instant gratification is something of a selling point — but it’s also a myth. Yes, they save an enormous amount of work compared with traditional astrophotography equipment. There’s no separate tracking mount to align, no camera to attach and no laptop required to control the imaging process. However, automation doesn’t necessarily mean instant results.

For example, every time the Vespera 3 is switched on, it needs to establish its position by identifying stars overhead. Its Star Zone Search and autofocus procedure took around five minutes, with a percentage displayed in the app to show how far it had progressed. That’s not an unreasonable wait for a sophisticated astronomical instrument, but it felt a little drawn-out when I was eager to begin photographing something. If there are clouds, expect it to take much longer.

Once the Vespera 3 had aligned itself, I could choose a target and leave the telescope to work. The optical arm moved into position, the camera began collecting exposures and an image gradually appeared on my smartphone.

I was less impressed by the touch-sensitive power button. Its softly illuminated indicator didn’t always make it obvious whether the telescope was switched on. More than once, I had to check my phone’s available Wi-Fi networks to establish whether it was on or off.

Vaonis claims the Vespera 3 can operate for up to 11 hours. I didn’t run it continuously until the battery was exhausted, but it lasted longer than every observing session I attempted. That did change how I used it, because I could concentrate on the target instead of keeping an eye on the remaining charge or wondering whether I should connect a portable battery.

The new, improved tripod also makes a difference. It’s tall, adjustable and reassuringly stable, with a useful canopy strung between its legs for holding any accessories — perhaps filters, a red torch or snacks.

The Vespera 3 is capable of photographing the moon and the sun, although solar photography requires a properly fitted optional solar filter. Unfortunately, that costs a further $179/£159, which is rather steep.

It’s also not the best choice for detailed planetary images. The 245mm focal length is ideal for framing many galaxies and nebulas, but Jupiter and Saturn remain small subjects.

Another omission is an equatorial tracking mode. Some cheaper smart telescopes — such as the Seestar S50 Pro and the DwarfLab Dwarf 3 — offer EQ mode for more advanced imaging, but the Vespera 3 relies solely on its motorized alt-azimuth mount. That doesn’t stop it from producing excellent photographs, but it does mean more experienced users have one less option to experiment with.

The biggest question surrounding the Vespera 3 isn’t whether it works — it’s whether it’s worth the money. After all, it costs far more than the Seestar S50 Pro, which also has built-in imaging filters, whereas the Vespera’s light pollution ($229/£219), dual-band ($399/£370) and solar (£179/£159) filters are optional purchases. They do, however, make a significant difference — with the dual-band filter giving nebulas more contrast, color and detail.

Overall, the Vespera 3 offers a slightly more polished imaging experience than the many entry-level smart telescopes on the market. I enjoyed its clean, colorful images and appreciated the ability to work on the same subject over several nights, while the excellent tripod and battery endurance make it particularly well suited to longer observing sessions.

I wouldn’t recommend it to everyone, but I can see why someone who already loves photographing the night sky might happily pay extra for the Vespera 3.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#783. Pregnant Brittany Mahomes Attends Chiefs Game After Sharing Baby News

Brittany Mahomes made her first appearance since revealing she's pregnant with her and Patrick Mahomes' fourth baby by supporting her husband at the Kansas City Chiefs game Nov. 15,

Brittany Mahomes is entering her pregnancy season once again.

Five days after the wife of Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes revealed she’s expecting the couple’s fourth child, she made her first public appearance since sharing the exciting news, stepping out to cheer on her husband in his NFL game against the Atlanta Falcons in Atlanta Nov. 15.

For the occasion, Brittany—who shares kids Sterling, 5, Bronze, 3, and Golden, 21 months, with Patrick—wore a Chiefs red jacket and oversized black sunglasses, styling her blond locks in a wavy ponytail.

And, of course, the 31-year-old brought her winning team to support Patrick on the field.

After all, Brittany shared fun videos of her kids enjoying some family fun before the Chiefs and the Falcons faced off.

In an adorable clip posted to her Instagram Stories Nov. 15, the Kansas City Current co-owner carried Golden through the stadium tunnel out onto the field, noting her daughter didn’t arrive empty-handed.

“This child literally walked into the stadium with [a] waffle in hand,” Brittany shared as her youngest ate her snack. “No waffle left behind!”

And just like her mom, the toddler arrived at the game in style, wearing a white jacket that featured her dad’s name and jersey number in red on her back, along with matching red ruffled leggings.

Golden matched with her older sister Sterling, who also sported Chiefs red leggings under a pink dress.

And as the Mahomes crew huddled up to watch Patrick score another win for the Chiefs, they are continuing to celebrate the exciting news of adding another player to their team.

On Nov. 10, Brittany and Patrick announced they’re expecting their fourth baby together.

“Another blessing from God,” the couple wrote in a joint Instagram post alongside sweet family photos, including a shot of their kids with their hands on Brittany’s baby bump. “& then there were 6.”

Though the pair—who tied the knot in 2022—haven’t shared whether they’re expecting a boy or girl, Patrick joked that he has one play he may prefer.

As the 31-year-old told reporters during a Nov. 11 press conference, “I’m hoping that me and Bronze can even up the score.”

But Patrick emphasized that all that matters is that his and Brittany’s new arrival is “healthy.”

“Obviously, it’s a blessing to have another baby on the way,” he shared. “I’m excited for it.”

#782. Snubs & Surprises In the 2027 Grammy Nominations

Grammy voters always have a few surprises up their sleeves.

We all knew that the Olivias (Dean and Rodrigo) were going to get a lot of love from Grammy voters this year. And sure enough, when nominations for the 69th annual Grammy Awards were announced bright and early on Monday (Nov. 16), they both did. So did such other expected names as Taylor Swift, Bruno Mars and Rosalía.

And it’s hardly a surprise that women dominated the nominations, though the degree of that dominance is impressive. For the first time in Grammy history, the six artists with the most nominations are all women. RAYE leads with 11 nods, followed by Rosalía with nine nods, and then Phoebe Bridgers, Miranda Lambert, Ella Langley and Olivia Rodrigo, with seven each.

But that doesn’t mean there were no surprises in the nominations. It’s impossible to have 100 categories without having at least a few outcomes that don’t land as expected. This year, nearly 16,000 voting members of the Recording Academy were eligible to vote. That includes more than 2,300 new voting members who joined as part of the 2026 new member class.

Final-round voting will take place from Dec. 10 to Jan. 7. The 69th annual Grammy Awards will air on Sunday, Feb. 7, at a new time – 7 p.m. ET/ 4 p.m. PT. The move was designed to let Grammy watchers on the East Coast watch the full show without having to stay up to midnight.

Here are some of the most notable snubs and surprises from the 69th annual Grammy nominations list.

Many expected Kahan to be nominated for album, record and song of the year, but he was completely overlooked in all three of those marquee categories. His only nod was for The Great Divide: The Last of the Bugs (the deluxe edition of his Billboard 200-topping album), which is nominated for best contemporary folk album. Whatever the reasons, after a few years of being one of the top music artists in America, Kahan has received a grand total of three Grammy nods. He might do well to remind himself of this truth, nicely articulated by a talented troubadour: “California’s so much more than some awards show.”

Antonoff received three nods – album of the year for Phoebe Bridgers’ Lost Weekend and song of the year and best song written for visual media for “I Knew It, I Knew You,” his collab with Taylor Swift. But he was passed over for a nod for producer of the year, non-classical for the third year in a row.

The jazz pianist, composer and bandleader died in February 2021, but he just keeps piling up Grammy nominations. He received two more this year – best jazz instrumental album for Forever Yours: The Farewell Performance (Live) and best arrangement, instrumental or a cappella for “Overjoyed (Live).” Corea has won six of his 29 Grammys since he died.

Lefty had one of the year’s biggest pop/country crossover hits with “Boston,” but was bypassed in the CMA Awards nominations and now is also omitted from the Grammy nominations. The accusations of plagiarism that tarnished her breakthrough moment likely kept voters from supporting her.

Some speculated that the talented brother and sister might both receive best new artist nominations in the same year, which would have been a Grammy Awards first. Neither did.

These three artists were in the conversation for best new artist, but few expected them to actually make it. But all three did make it. The Womack Sisters are the first sister act to be nominated since Chloe x Halle (Bailey) eight years ago. Zeimani, Zekkujcha, and Zekuumba Womack are daughters of musicians Linda and Cecil Womack, members of the R&B duo Womack & Womack, and nieces of singer Bobby Womack and granddaughters of singer Sam Cooke.

Both artists were touted as best new artist hopefuls; both fell short. Fender had a long-running Hot 100 hit with “Rein Me In,” but voters may have figured anybody could have a Hot 100 hit at this point if they teamed up with the red-hot Olivia Dean. Role Model’s failure to receive a nod may be due to voters expecting a stronger follow-up to his irresistible late 2025 viral hit “Sally, When the Wine Runs Out.”

Summit’s sophomore album, Ctrl Escape, was blanked in the nominations. Summit’s camp had submitted the album for best dance/electronic album, and two of its tracks in other categories – “Lights Go Out” for best dance/electronic recording and “Don’t Believe It” (with Absolutely) for best dance pop recording. Summit expressed his displeasure on X, saying “the whole dance category is just music industry fueled pop stars” rather than a celebration of authentic electronic music culture. Summit (who promoted his 2024 album Comfort in Chaos with a performance and interview at the Grammy Museum in L.A.) declared he will never submit his music to the Recording Academy again unless significant changes are made to how electronic/dance music is judged.

never submitting to the grammys again unless shit changes, it’s all a fucking joke. i’m not just talking about myself either there’s zero respect for real electronic dance music & dj’s. the whole dance category is just music industry fueled pop stars

Spiro is nominated for best new artist, as widely expected, but her elegant ballad “Die on This Hill” was passed over for both record and song of the year nods. Not a shock – the record peaked at No. 19 on the Hot 100, a bit low to register in such a competitive category – but it had echoes of Adele’s breakthrough hit “Chasing Pavements,” which was nominated in both categories in 2009.

Wicked: For Good didn’t receive a single Oscar nomination earlier this year, but Grammy voters supported the project. The album is up for best compilation soundtrack for visual media, while “No Place Like Home” is up for best song written for visual media and Cynthia Erivo and Ariana Grande’s collaboration on “For Good” is nominated for best traditional pop vocal performance. Last year, the first Wicked was nominated for best compilation soundtrack, while “Defying Gravity” won a Grammy for best pop duo/group performance.

#781. An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution

An extraordinary collection of fossils in central Colombia is revealing a surprising chapter in Earth's evolutionary history. Researchers have uncovered evidence of a time when ancient animal groups that were approaching extinction lived alongside newer groups that would eventually flourish. The discovery suggests that major evolutionary transitions can occur without the widespread destruction associated with mass extinctions.

Scientists from McGill University and the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) identified this unusual pattern while studying fossils from Colombia's Paja Formation. The ancient marine ecosystem preserves an exceptional mixture of surviving Jurassic lineages and emerging Cretaceous groups, offering a rare glimpse into a period of profound biological change.

Drawing on these findings, McGill biology professor Hans Larsson and PhD graduate Dirley Cortés have proposed a new concept called a "Biotic Inflection." The term describes an evolutionary turning point when older groups nearing extinction coexist with newer lineages that are beginning to expand and diversify.

A Perfect Storm for Ancient Ocean Biodiversity

The researchers believe an unusual combination of environmental conditions helped make this remarkable coexistence possible. Warm greenhouse temperatures, elevated sea levels, and coastal waters rich in nutrients may have supported an unusually diverse range of marine life.

Another important factor was the emergence of new ocean connections between the eastern Pacific and the early Atlantic through the region that is now Colombia. Together, these conditions likely created opportunities for different groups of animals to thrive within the same ecosystem. Many of these environmental influences continue to shape biodiversity around the world today.

"The Paja Formation records an extraordinary process in the history of life, when a 'perfect storm' of environmental factors we know to promote ecological complexity coincided with ancient lineages that were about to disappear. At the same time, new groups were beginning to flourish," Larsson said.

A Lost World of Giant Marine Reptiles and Predators

The evidence comes from the Early Cretaceous Paja Formation near Villa de Leyva, Colombia. This fossil-rich region has preserved an astonishing variety of prehistoric marine animals, providing scientists with an unusually detailed picture of an ancient ocean ecosystem. Most of the fossils collected from the formation are housed at the CIP.

"This geological formation has produced an exceptionally rich fossil record that includes giant marine reptiles like long-necked plesiosaurs and marine crocodile relatives, as well as turtles, sharks, crustaceans and others," Cortés explained. "Together, these animals formed the Paja Biota, one of the most ecologically complex marine communities found to date."

In a previous study, the researchers reconstructed the feeding relationships among animals in the Paja Biota. Their analysis revealed an exceptionally intricate food web, with an unusually large variety of apex predators occupying the highest levels of the ecosystem.

This remarkable complexity makes the Paja Formation especially valuable for investigating how ecosystems change as older evolutionary groups decline and new ones become established.

Could This Discovery Change How Scientists Understand Evolution?

The proposed Biotic Inflection offers a potentially important new way to understand major changes in Earth's biodiversity. Rather than being driven by a mass extinction, some evolutionary transitions may involve periods of extraordinary diversity, when declining lineages and emerging groups coexist.

However, the researchers emphasize that more evidence is needed to establish how common this pattern may have been. Additional fossil discoveries, more accurate estimates of fossil ages, and comparisons with geological formations in other parts of the world will help determine whether similar transitions occurred elsewhere in Earth's history.

"I think we've discovered a new model of global biodiversity change. Now we'll need to see just how widespread this could be in Earth's history and how we can quantify its impacts," Larsson said.

The research received funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, the Anders Foundation, the 1923 Fund, Gregory D. and Jennifer Walston Johnson, the Fonds de recherche Nature et technologies Québec, and the McGill Biology Department Writing-Year Award 2024-2025.

#780. Why Taylor Swift's Showgirl Encore Album Isn’t Eligible for Grammys

Though Taylor Swift’s “Patient Zero” broke records this year, the song and its album The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore aren’t eligible for the 2027 Grammys because of the Recording Academy’s rules.

Taylor Swift’s latest album won’t go in the blank space of Grammys ballots.

That’s because The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore—the deluxe version of her The Life of a Showgirl album—doesn’t qualify for the 2027 Grammys for multiple reasons.

First, for a song or album to be eligible for the upcoming Grammys, which will be handed out in February 2027, it would have needed to be released within the eligibility window of Aug. 31, 2025, to Aug. 28, 2026.

But since the extended version of Swift’s album was released on Sept. 25, it falls outside of eligibility for the 2027 Grammys.

But even the following year, the Encore album, with its four new songs, still won’t be eligible for Album of the Year if rules remain the same. That’s because the Grammys’ Recording Academy now requires that new recordings make up at least 66 percent of an album—a decrease from the previous threshold of 75 percent—in order to qualify.

But that worry you feel for Swift’s Grammy hopes? You can shake it off.

Her new tracks “Patient Zero,” “Pink Clouding,” “Babylon” and “Cleveland!” will be eligible for consideration at the 2028 show for categories that recognize individual songs.

And of course, the original Life of a Showgirl album—released in October 2025—is up for all categories at the 2027 Grammys.

Meanwhile, Swift’s song “I Knew It, I Knew You,” which she wrote for Toy Story 5, isn’t just collecting teardrops on the guitars of fans—it could also bring home trophies for Song of the Year, Best Song Written for Visual Media, Best Country Song, Best Country Solo Performance and other categories, if nominated.

“Writing this song felt like a musical departure and coming home at the same time,” the “Anti-Hero” singer wrote on Instagram in June. “Creating something for Jessie was a new challenge and also felt like second nature all at once.”

She also shared her appreciation for the movie’s director, adding, “Thank you to the brilliant Andrew Stanton for imagining me for this, all those years ago when you wrote this newest film.”

To learn what—and who—inspired many of Swift’s other songs, keep reading…

Before The Life of a Showgirl, the only track Taylor had certainly written about her guy on the Chiefs—save for The Eras Tour “Karma” rewrite, of course—is “So High School,” which the now-engaged couple aptly set their proposal Instagram post to in August 2025.

Although some fans speculate “The Alchemy,” also off The Tortured Poets Department, is about Travis for the football and high school metaphors sprinkled in the track, “So High School” includes a more obvious nod with the lyrics: “Are you going to marry, kiss or kill me? / It’s just a game but really / I’m betting on all three, for us two.”

Indeed, Travis revealed to AfterBuzzTV back in 2016 that “Taylor Swift, would be the kiss,” in a game of “Marry, Kiss, Kill” between her, Ariana Grande and Katy Perry.

As for how Travis feels about the track? Although it’s a tough competition as a Swiftie, it’s his all-time favorite.

“I’m not gonna lie,” he joked of the choice to Access Hollywood in 2024. “I might be a little biased.”

But now that Taylor has found the guy who can call her honey, he's the one she most wants to pay tribute to in verse.

On The Life of a Showgirl, she sang about her now-husband topping her "Wi$h Li$t," serving as her "forever night stand" in "Honey," and turning her sky "Opalite."

And, forgive her, it sounds cocky, but in "Wood," her raciest song yet, she shared how Travis' love was the key that opened her thighs.

Fortunately, Taylor's mom Andrea Swift, "thinks that the song is about superstitions, which it absolutely is," Taylor joked on SiriusXM’s Morning Mash Up after the album's October 2025 release. "That’s the joy of the double entendre. You can read that song for people, and it just goes right over their heads."

But it wasn't hard to grasp who she was calling "the love of my life" on the Encore track "Cleveland!," the title itself an overt nod to Travis' hometown.

Although short-lived, Taylor appeared to write several songs on The Tortured Poets Department about her dalliance with The 1975 frontman in 2023, including the album’s title track which also name drops their mutual pal and collaborator Jack Antonoff.

Other tracks rumored to be about Matty include “Fortnight,” “Down Bad,” and “But Daddy I Love Him,” the latter of which also appears to call out the backlash Taylor received for her relationship with him.

And while Matty told paparazzi, per Entertainment Tonight in 2024 that he hadn’t listened to the album, though he was "sure it’s good," his mother Denise Welch slammed his alleged connection to the breakup ballads.

"You're not allowed to say anything," the Loose Woman cohost said during a 2025 appearance on Watch What Happens Live, "and then she writes a whole album about it."

For more on Matty’s place in Taylor’s catalogue, read here.

It's actually sweet all the time an unnamed rival has spent on the singer. Or, at least, that's what Taylor conveyed in The Life of a Showgirl track "Actually Romantic."

Rather than share her praise for Travis or even an ex-lover, the musician actually sings about a person who "high-fived my ex and then you said you're glad he ghosted me. Wrote me a song saying it makes you sick to see my face / Some people might be offended / But it's actually sweet."

Fans were quick to say the clues pointed toward Charli XCX, who opened for Taylor on her Reputation Tour and is close with Taylor's ex Matty and his now-wife Gabbriette Bechtel.

Another tell was Charli's 2024 brat track "Sympathy Is a Knife," in which the British musician—married to Matty's The 1975 bandmate George Daniel—sings, "Don’t wanna see her backstage at my boyfriend’s show. Fingers crossed behind my back / I hope they break up real quick."

Good thing for Brittany Mahomes, Taylor likes her friends canceled. Because fans feel the singer was thinking of the former soccer player—wed to Travis' teammate Patrick Mahomes—or onetime BFF Blake Lively when she wrote about standing by a pal's side when the whole world has seemingly turned on them.

But really the person at the crux of The Life of a Showgirl track is Taylor herself, who felt her reputation took several hits after her very public 2016 feud with Kanye West and then-wife Kim Kardashian.

"Having had my own experiences with mass judgment and being at the center of many dramatic, scandalous moments in my career, where people were all weighing in at once or at least it felt like that," she told Amazon Music, "having had those experiences, it makes me move through the world a little bit differently."

And now she wants to gift that what-doesn't-kill-you-makes-you-stronger mentality to others. As the lyrics suggest, Taylor continued, "I don't just naturally cast people aside just because other people decide they don't like them. I make my own decisions about people based on how they treat me within my life and their actions."

Amid their six-year relationship, Taylor penned several songs about—and with—the Conversations With Friends star. Shortly after the pair's relationship was confirmed in 2016, she released Reputation, which included several songs presumably about Joe such as “Call It What You Want,” “Dress,” and “King of My Heart.”

On Lover, Taylor also included the track "Cornelia Street," a nod to the New York City rental she was living in during the early months of their romance. Elsewhere in her discography, fans believe Taylor also penned "invisible string," on folklore about her romance with Joe, as well as Midnights' "Sweet Nothing" and its bonus track 'You’re Losing Me," which her producer Jack confirmed was written two years before Taylor's 2023 breakup with Joe.

Joe is one of the many people in Taylor’s life who has also become her cowriter on songs, earning credits on folklore and evermore songs like "betty," "champagne problems," "exile" and others under the pseudonym William Bowery.

"It was really the most accidental thing to happen in lockdown," the Brutalist alum told GQ of the cowriting credits in 2022. "It was just messing around on a piano and singing badly and being overheard and then thinking, you know, what if we tried to get to the end of it together?"

For more songs inspired by Joe, see here.

Following the infamous—and later revealed to be edited—phone call leak in 2016 between Kanye and Taylor over a reference he made to her on his The Life of Pablo album, Taylor has subtly clapped back at the divorced couple more than once.

As recently as 2024, Taylor penned "thanK you aIMee" likely about Kim, given she capitalized letters in the track's title to spell out her name. (In another variant of the TTPD album, she changed the letters to capitalize "YE" in the track, as an apparent nod toward the rapper.)

Prior to TTPD, Taylor also sprinkled hits against Kim and Kanye for the "Famous" feud, with "Mad Woman," on folklore, where she sings, "Women like hunting witches too / Doing your dirtiest work for you / It’s obvious that wanting me dead has really brought you two together."

Taylor’s first Reputation single "Look What You Made Me Do," was also a nod to the public fallout, as well as "This Is Why We Can’t Have Nice Things," in which she sings about a once-repaired friendship fracturing again.

But, of course, Taylor's musical inspirations from Kanye date back to that 2009 MTV VMA incident, when he interrupted her speech for Best Female Video at the Video Music Awards. In Speak Now’s "Innocent," she forgives Kanye for the viral moment, which earned him backlash from figures as prominent as then-president Barack Obama.

"It's OK / Life is a tough crowd," Taylor sings on the track, going on to reference his age at the time of the VMAs. "32 and still growing up now / Who you are is not what you did / You’re still an innocent."

For a thorough dive into Taylor’s beef with Kanye, see here.

Taylor and the Loki actor may have only had a short-lived romance in the summer of 2016, but it did inspire more than one track for the "Karma" singer. Indeed, many fans speculated that "Getaway Car," and "High Infidelity" are about the timeline of their romance in comparison to her relationship with Calvin Harris. She and the DJ split in June 2016 after one year of dating, the same month she sparked rumors with Tom.

In both songs, Taylor sings about how a relationship born out of slight infidelity is doomed from the start.

While fans are sure these three are the ones who made up the "Getaway Car" sideshow, neither Taylor, nor Calvin or Tom have addressed the inspiration for the songs.

Although Taylor shut down any speculation that she wrote songs about her romance with the One Direction alum, there are a lot of subtle references to the "Watermelon Sugar" singer on 1989.

"Style," is the most obvious nod to Harry, simply for the title, as well as "Out of the Woods," and bonus track "Wonderland," which references a "Cheshire cat smile"—which many fans see as a nod to Harry’s hometown of Holmes Chapel in Cheshire, England.

Meanwhile, the 1989 vault track "Is It Over Now?" paints a vivid picture of the moment Taylor knew her romance with Harry was done for good.

"Blue dress on a boat," she sings in reference to the infamous January 2013 photo of her after the couple’s alleged breakup in the Virgin Islands. "Your new girl is my clone."

On "Now That We Don’t Talk," she references the doomed vacation again, and slams Harry’s infamous music taste in the lines, "I don’t have to pretend I like acid rock / Or that I’d like to be on a mega-yacht."

And while Taylor went on to date several more stars from across the pond, Harry was her first British bloke. And since London is referenced in other songs in her earlier catalogue, including Red’s "Come Back, Be Here" and "Message in a Bottle," the tracks are also speculated to be about Harry.

Harry didn’t earn the entirety of 1989’s inspiration. Indeed, many fans believe the track "Bad Blood" is about Katy as Taylor teased to Rolling Stone in 2014 it was about another "female artist," who "tried to sabotage an entire arena tour."

"I was like, 'Oh, we’re just straight-up enemies,'" Taylor, who at the time saw some of her background dancers leave for Katy's Prismatic tour, added. "It wasn’t even about a guy! It had to do with business."

However, Taylor maintained she penned the song simply to get some feelings off her chest.

"My intent was not to create some gossip-fest," she added to Rolling Stone. "I wanted people to apply it to a situation where they felt betrayed in their own lives."

Ultimately, though, the song fueled a feud—with Katy posting on X one day after the Rolling Stone piece published, "Watch out for Regina George in sheep’s clothing."

The singers were later able to squash their beef in 2019, after which Katy made a cameo in Taylor’s "You Need to Calm Down" music video.

Taylor can write fanfiction, too. Ahead of the release of Red, Taylor met Ethel while dating her grandson Conor Kennedy, and ultimately penned the song "Starlight" about a reimagined version of a date night between the Kennedy matriarch and her late husband.

"Starlight is a song that I wrote after seeing a picture of Ethel and Bobby Kennedy when they were 17," Taylor explained in a Red interview. "I didn’t know anything about what they were doing or what was going on in the picture, but I just thought 'They look like they’re having the best night.' And so I wrote this song about what the night might’ve been like."

In response to the nod, Ethel told the Cape Cod Times, "She is just sensational, inside and out."

One of Taylor’s most popular breakup songs of all time "All Too Well"—and its 10-minute alternate version—is thought to be about the Donnie Darko star. After all, it references autumn—when their short-lived 2010 romance took place—her subject’s sister’s house, and a certain scarf. (Jake, of course, has a very famous sister in Maggie Gyllenhaal, and the duo passed a striped Gucci scarf between them during their romance.)

Taylor also appeared to take shots at her romance with Jake in "The Last Time," "We Are Never Getting Back Together," and the Red vault track "I Bet You Think About Me," which call out the subject’s music taste and wealthy background.

Despite widespread belief Red as a whole was mostly inspired by Jake, he shut down any connection following the album’s 2021 rerelease.

"It’s about her relationship with her fans," he told Esquire in 2022. "It is her expression."

Taylor, meanwhile, did concur with Jake's sentiment, noting that she saw "All Too Well" become something much deeper than a breakup song.

"What was so crazy is that when it went out into the world, the fans just among themselves decided it was their favorite too," she explained on Good Morning America in 2021.  "They just sort of ... claimed it as the most important song from Red...over the course of the first six months the album was out."

Many fans speculate that The Tortured Poets Department's "The Manuscript" is about the impact of "All Too Well," and thus, Taylor's relationship with Jake.

Yes, at least half of Taylor’s heart—at the age of 19, anyway—once belonged to the "Gravity" musician. And it possibly led to some of her Speak Now tracks like "Dear John," and "The Story of Us," which Taylor previously revealed were inspired by the same person.

"'The Story of Us' is about running into someone I had been in a relationship with at an awards show, and we were seated a few seats away from each other," she told USA Today in 2010. "I just wanted to say to him, 'Is this killing you? Because it's killing me.' But I didn't. Because I couldn't. Because we both had these silent shields up."

While Taylor has said she doesn’t use Easter eggs to hint at her personal life, the "Story of Us" liner notes—where Taylor used to hide messages for her fans—on the original Speak Now album spelled out "CMT Awards," an event she and John both attended in 2010.

As for where "Dear John" is concerned? John himself had to respond to the brazen shots fired.

"I didn’t deserve it," the musician told Rolling Stone in 2012. "I'm pretty good at taking accountability now, and I never did anything to deserve that. It was a really lousy thing for her to do."

Once too young to be messed with, Taylor is now too wise to be bothered with any drama. "I don’t care about anything that happened to me when I was 19," she told fans ahead of playing "Dear John," at The Eras Tour in 2023. "Except for the songs that I wrote and the memories we made together."

As she put it, “I do not care. We’ve all grown up. We’re good.”

Following a 2009 romance with the Twilight star, Taylor penned "Back to December" about the relationship. In addition to alluding to a "September night" where her subject saw her cry (Lautner was also at the 2009 VMAs), she included a nod to him in the song’s liner notes, which read, "Tay."

Ahead of Speak Now's rerelease in 2023, the Sharkboy and Lava Girl alum joked about his role in the album’s songs, telling Today at the time, "I feel safe."

Some fans also speculate that "Today Was a Fairytale" and "I Can See You"—the music video he starred in—were about her Valentine’s Day costar as well, as in the latter track, Taylor sings about keeping "everything professional," before a romance ensued.

Believe it or not, Taylor once got butterflies from the "Fireflies" singer. "Enchanted" is about a night she met the frontman for Owl City, and she revealed she included the line "wonderstruck" so he’d know it was about him, as he had used the word in an email to her.

"Meeting him," Taylor told Yahoo in 2010. "It was this overwhelming feeling of: I really hope that you’re not in love with somebody."

A year later, Adam responded to the musical love letter by rerecording the song, adding in his own lyrics, "Oh Taylor, I was so enchanted to meet you too."

"I'll be the first to admit I’m a rather shy boy and since music is the most eloquent form of communication I can muster, I decided to record something for you–a sort of a 'reply' to the breathtaking song on your current record," he added in a note beneath the song, shared to his band's website at the time. "You are a true princess from a dreamy fairy tale."

Once upon a time, Taylor was extremely up front when it came to who inspired her songs, especially where her breakup with Joe Jonas is concerned. Back in 2008, she quickly penned "Forever and Always" and tacked it on as a last-minute addition to Fearless, perfectly timed to her infamous appearance on Ellen, where she called out the Jonas Brothers member for breaking up with her in a 27-second phone call.

On her next album, Speak Now, released in 2010, Taylor included two nods to Joe, including "Last Kiss," a heart-wrenching ballad which references July 9, a.k.a. the date of the 2008 Jonas Brothers concert she attended while she and Joe were still together.

Elsewhere on the album, Taylor included "Better Than Revenge," which was a clap back at the Jonas Brothers’ song "Much Better," which had a not-so-veiled reference to her in the lyric, "I'm done with superstars and all the tears on her guitar."

Later on in her discography, Taylor included fonder nods to her past romance with Joe on Red’s "Holy Ground," and folklore’s "Invisible String," the latter in which she reflects on becoming friendly with him in more recent years. "Cold was the steel of my axe to grind for the boys who broke my heart," she sings in the song, "Now I send their babies presents."

However, when Taylor released Fearless (Taylor’s Version) in 2021, she gave Joe one more whack with "Mr. Perfectly Fine," though she penned the song around the time of their 2008 breakup. It was Joe’s now-ex-wife Sophie Turner who seemingly confirmed the track was about her then-husband, sharing the song to social media at the time and joking, "It's not NOT a bop."

A commercial satellite has spotted the International Space Station (ISS), giving us a unique view of the orbiting lab from above.

Most of the time, when we see the ISS, it is from down here on Earth or from the viewpoint of the astronauts onboard, peering out the windows at the station's limbs, solar arrays and instruments.

But in this snapshot, which was posted on X on Nov. 9 by the Australian company HEO, we can see the station stretched out in all its glory.

HEO specializes in using satellites in low Earth orbit to capture images of other spacecraft, though longer-term the company aims to capture observations far out into the solar system. HEO doesn't build the satellites that take these photos; rather, the company's software tasks the spacecraft to image targets as they come into range.

This great photo of the ISS from above, for example, was taken by a satellite operated by BlackSky, a Virginia-based company that holds a non-Earth imaging agreement with HEO.

So far, HEO and its partners have captured imagery of a variety of spacecraft in orbit, including the ISS, China's Tiangong space station and the European Space Agency's ERS-2 satellite (while it was hurtling back to Earth in 2024).

While it might seem that satellites are just hovering above Earth, the space station and other spacecraft in LEO are hurtling through space at roughly 17,500 mph (28,160 kph), hundreds of miles above our planet's surface.

A snapshot of a satellite from above is therefore far from mundane. Rather, it requires incredible coordination and technical skill; satellite operators must know precisely when their target will present itself, and their equipment must be capable of getting the shot.
